title: Principles for Inclusive Classrooms
author: Ben Newmark
summary: Ben Newmark tackles the ambiguity of "inclusion" as a term in school culture, arguing that on its own the word means nothing - it only becomes meaningful through concrete examples of what counts as included or excluded in a specific context. He builds a working definition specific to classrooms, where the primary purpose is learning: a child present in every lesson but silently drawing instead of engaging, or daydreaming unnoticed, has not actually been included even though they were physically there. Central to his argument is reframing inclusion as a fluctuating continuum rather than a fixed threshold to cross, which he says removes the moral judgment baked into the word and allows more honest professional conversations about small, achievable improvements rather than an impossible permanent state. He then directly confronts the pluralistic vision of inclusive classrooms - individualised tasks, materials, and environments for different learners simultaneously - tracing it to now-discredited learning-styles theory and arguing it doesn't scale to a mainstream class of nearly thirty students the way it might for a private tutor working one-on-one. Turning to SEND specifically, Newmark argues that when you actually read pupil passports and EHC plans, the strategies listed - consistent routines, breaking tasks into steps, checking for understanding - are simply features of strong teaching generally, not evidence that the roughly 40% of children identified with SEND at some point require fundamentally different instruction; even dyslexia-specific reading interventions, he notes, mostly sharpen common principles rather than replace them.
points: Newmark's foundational move is definitional: he argues inclusion is meaningless as a standalone word and only gains content through concrete classroom examples, since two schools claiming to be inclusive can mean entirely different things.

He reframes inclusion as a continuum rather than a threshold - a classroom can be more inclusive Monday than Wednesday - which he argues removes the moral coding that makes inclusive a loaded, defensiveness-triggering label in staff conversations.

Newmark directly challenges the pluralistic-learning-styles vision of inclusion (different children on different tasks, materials, environments simultaneously), arguing it lacks evidence and doesn't scale to a mainstream class of nearly thirty children.

He argues most SEND-labelled strategies (consistent routines, breaking tasks into steps, checking for understanding) are simply good teaching practice for everyone, not evidence that roughly 40% of children genuinely require radically different instruction.
quotes: It is hard to talk about things when people don’t have a shared understanding of the words they use, and words usually don’t mean anything on their own – terminology is only given meaning through practical examples.

If a history teacher fails to spot a child is drawing anime characters in their jotter instead of answering a question on the feudal system, they are not included. If a child daydreams away the day and nobody intervenes, they’ve not been included even if they have been present in every lesson.

Neither inclusion nor exclusion are fixed states, and so trying to become inclusive as if this were a threshold to cross is to set an impossible aim, because the conditions affecting it change all the time
Instead of trying to become “inclusive”, teachers should aim to be more inclusive more of the time and work on strategies and practices that make this more likely.
Teachers aren’t private tutors, and don’t typically teach children one-on-one, which makes teaching strategies designed to work in this context of limited use to a typical mainstream teacher

It is possible I’m overreaching, and I’m open to the possibility there may be some circumstances and conditions in which to be inclusive teaching must be extensively adapted but it is implausible most of the approximately 40% of children identified as having a SEND need

For example, for most children with dyslexia methods of reading instruction aren’t different to children who do not have dyslexia, and when instruction is adapted this is to make the common principles more precise and targeted.
